A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and provide readable main text, equations, figures, and appendices. Corresponding content can be matched despite restructuring and appendix renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments, gradient and loss-landscape measurements, and appendix analyses of noise, model size, computational budgets, and horizon scheduling.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds Amazon stock forecasting results in Figure 5.

M1.justification: The MLP architectures and adaptive horizon/learning-rate mechanism are retained. Algorithm 1 changes its written termination condition from elapsed time below T_max to below T_max*s, introducing s=k_max/T_max. This is a limited procedural revision, although its units and implementation remain unclear.

E1.justification: v3 adds Amazon stock prices from 1997–2017 to the four synthetic systems and two climate datasets. This extends coverage into financial forecasting and explicitly tests nonstationary data whose values extend beyond the training range, materially broadening the evaluated conditions.

E2.justification: The adaptive scheduler is still compared with fixed-horizon, constant-learning-rate training in Figure 12. Newly discussed RNNs, Transformers, and PatchTST are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: The added AMZN experiment evaluates MSE across training horizons of 1–5 days. Algorithm 1 also changes its reported time-budget condition, without establishing that existing experiments were rerun. Retained synthetic sampling intervals, climate splits, and five-step climate evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.1 adds AMZN as a limited stress case explicitly violating stationarity and state-coverage assumptions. Existing noise, model-size, learning-rate, compute-budget, and scheduling analyses remain in the renumbered appendices G–I.

E5.justification: Median/interquartile summaries and boxplots were already reported in v1. The AMZN results follow the existing reporting practice; v3 supplies no new seed information, repeated-run counts, confidence-interval procedure, or significance testing.

E6.justification: Figure 5 adds AMZN results, with the lowest plotted median MSE around 2–3-day training horizons and substantial overlapping variability. Existing synthetic, climate, noise, and scheduling results are retained; the addition does not establish a same-setting performance improvement over v1.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.8 develops embedding, context-window, and recurrent-state lemmas and a proposition for partial observability. Definition 4.1 changes its domain from the observed-state convex hull to stationary-distribution support, and Appendix A.4 revises the gradient derivation. Equation 3 becomes explicitly quadratic, consistent with the already reported MSE experiments. Remark A.21 leaves full extensions of the loss-landscape proofs undeveloped.

C1.justification: The central performance–learnability trade-off and three principal contributions remain. v3's conclusion explicitly extends the anticipated applicability to RNNs and Transformers with long-term dependencies, while removing v1's introductory dismissal of memory architectures as unnecessarily complex for the considered systems.

C2.justification: Section 4.4 and Appendix B substantially expand the discussion of assumptions and applicability. Remark 4.8 clarifies that increasing extrema along parameter-space lines need not imply more full-dimensional minima. Section 5.2 adds an explanation of why compute-dependent optimal horizons complicate hyperparameter search, and Appendix A.21 identifies the unfinished steps in extending the theory.

D1.justification: Figures 2 and 3 newly describe one-step initial training, continued training, and the selection of separated late checkpoints; Figure 9 newly states per-panel normalization. v1's promise to provide code upon acceptance disappears without replacement access instructions. Existing architecture, hardware, and climate-processing details are retained.

R1.justification: v3 explicitly attributes preceding gradient-growth results to Mikhaeil et al. (2022), distinguishing them from the paper's loss-geometry contribution. It adds targeted connections to embedding and Transformer literature, including Deco and Schürmann, Nie et al., and Zeng et al., while removing several general architecture references.

P1.justification: The related-work and background sections undergo substantial rewriting. v3 separates limitations and optimal-horizon selection into dedicated subsections, reorganizes discussion material, expands appendix explanations, and systematically distinguishes physical horizons T from autoregressive step counts K or k.

P2.justification: Figure 5 expands from two panels beside wrapped text to a full-width three-panel display. Several captions and axis labels change, including Figure 2's ratio label and Figure 10's step notation. Journal formatting changes headers, typography, and float placement, while most existing graphics retain their displays.

improvement.justification: Relative to v1, v3 better explains the theory's applicability, distinguishes cross-sectional extrema from full-dimensional minima, and credits preceding gradient results. These changes improve interpretation, while AMZN supplies a limited additional empirical check. The gains remain modest: full recurrent/Transformer extensions are deferred, the stock experiment lacks detailed protocol information, and the revised scheduler introduces ambiguous budget notation while the code-release statement disappears.
